faq.q: How does a cable-stayed bridge work?
faq.a: Straight steel cables called stays run from tall towers directly to the deck. The stays pull up on the deck and also squeeze it lengthways, which balances their pull, so no end anchorages are needed.
asks: How do stay cables hold a bridge?

faq.q: What is the difference between cable-stayed and suspension bridges?
faq.a: A cable-stayed bridge connects its deck straight to the towers with many straight cables. A suspension bridge hangs its deck from two big curved main cables that are anchored into the ground at both ends.
asks: How can I tell the bridges apart?

faq.q: What are fan and harp patterns?
faq.a: In a fan pattern the stays all meet near the top of the tower and spread out. In a harp pattern the stays are parallel, joining the tower at different heights.
asks: Why do bridge cables look different?

faq.q: Why are so many new bridges cable-stayed?
faq.a: They need less cable, no huge anchorages, and can be built outward from each tower without temporary supports. That makes them faster and cheaper for spans up to about a kilometre.

faq.q: Why are suspension bridges used for the longest spans?
faq.a: A cable-stayed deck is squeezed harder and harder as the span grows, and very long stays sag and lose stiffness. A suspension bridge's main cables keep working well beyond two kilometres.
asks: Why can't cable-stayed bridges be longer?

facts: Russky Bridge in Russia, opened in 2012, has a cable-stayed main span of 1,104 metres.
The Millau Viaduct in France, a cable-stayed bridge opened in 2004, is the tallest bridge in the world, with one mast top 343 metres above its base.

quiz.say: Which bridge type needs huge anchorages at both ends to hold its cables?
quiz.why: A suspension bridge's main cables pull hard at their ends, so they must be tied into massive anchorages.

wrong.0: A cable-stayed deck balances the pull of its stays itself, so no ground anchorages are needed.
wrong.2: A beam bridge has no cables at all.
